<reason>A won a close, high-quality clash by making the live voting issue institutional: who bears aquifer uncertainty and how costly it is to say no. B’s “creek doesn’t read the deed” turn was the sharpest single attack, especially after A allowed continued pumping under public contract, but A converted that into an opposite-default comparison CON never fully escaped. B’s better-instrument alternative still depended on writing and enforcing the permits both sides already treated as a repeated failure mode. Trade and private-takings costs remained live for B, yet more theoretical than A’s clearer reason to prefer a categorical rule.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s Rebuttal 2 answers to B’s well/creek questions: public title makes “no” a nonrenewal rather than a taking, so the same pump has the opposite default and the hydrology fight becomes unnecessary.</best_rebuttal>
